title: What Would You Do Differently If You Designed This Again?
summary: The self-critique question tests whether you can name a real weakness in your own design unprompted — before the interviewer has to find it for you.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"What would you do differently if you designed this again?"** It's a self-critique question, graded on whether you can name a real weakness in your own design unprompted — showing judgment while nothing is under pressure yet, before the interviewer has to surface the flaw themselves.

The reflex to avoid is claiming the design has no regrets. That reads as either dishonest (every real design involves trade-offs) or as a lack of self-awareness — both worse than admitting one specific, well-reasoned weakness.

Before answering, figure out what's actually being asked. Sometimes the interviewer is probing a decision you made under genuine uncertainty — an early trade-off where the right call wasn't obvious at the time. Other times they're fishing for whether you noticed a specific flaw that's already visible in the design you just presented, giving you a chance to catch it yourself before they point it out.

A quick clarifying question — "are you asking about a specific part of the design, or my overall approach?" — costs nothing and tells you which situation you're in, so your answer targets the right kind of weakness instead of a generic one.

The skeleton: pick one decision you made under real uncertainty, name specifically what you'd revisit with more information or time, and say exactly what evidence would have changed your original call.

This works because it's falsifiable — a vague answer like "I'd add more scalability" can't be checked against anything, but "I'd revisit consistency once I saw real read-latency numbers" names a concrete trigger. Pick the decision that was genuinely closest to a coin flip when you made it, not a random weak spot invented on the spot for the question.

A worked example: "I chose eventual consistency for the leaderboard because I assumed users wouldn't notice a few seconds of lag. With real traffic data, I'd want to check whether competitive players actually notice and complain — and if they do, I'd revisit toward stronger consistency for just that one feature, not the whole system."

Notice the shape: name the assumption, name the evidence that would test it, and scope the fix narrowly (just the leaderboard, not a system-wide rewrite) — that narrow scoping signals you're not overcorrecting to sound thorough.

A second worked example, this time about a capacity assumption rather than an architecture choice: "I sized the cache for 10x expected read traffic based on a rough estimate. I'd want real production numbers before committing that much memory — I might be over-provisioning and wasting budget, or under-provisioning and heading for an eviction problem under real load."

Capacity assumptions make good answers here because they're numerically checkable — you can name the exact metric (cache hit rate, memory headroom) that would prove your original guess right or wrong.

| | Vague weakness | Specific, falsifiable weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Example | "I'd add more monitoring" | "I'd specifically watch replication lag on leaderboard writes" |
| What it shows | Sounds responsible, reveals nothing about your judgment | Names the exact number that would tell you if the call was wrong |
| Interviewer's read | Safe, rehearsed, uninformative | You know precisely what you don't know yet |

**How to decide which weakness to lead with:** pick the one where you can name the exact metric or signal that would have changed your decision — if you can't name that signal, you haven't found a real weakness yet, just a generic hedge.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Naming a real weakness costs you a moment of looking less than perfect — you're handing the interviewer a place to dig further instead of leaving them nothing to push on. In exchange, you show you can evaluate your own work honestly, which is exactly the signal self-critique questions test for.

The alternative — claiming no regrets — avoids that momentary vulnerability but reads as either dishonest (every real design involves trade-offs made under incomplete information) or as a lack of judgment. Both readings are strictly worse than the discomfort of naming one real, specific weakness.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: why didn't you design it that way from the start?
slides.markdown:
A common follow-up: "why didn't you just design it that way from the start?" Defend the original trade-off honestly — it was the right call given the information and constraints you actually had then, not a mistake you're now backpedaling from.

Say specifically what would have needed to be true for you to choose differently upfront: for the leaderboard example, that's having real latency-sensitivity data before the design phase even started, which by definition wasn't available yet. This distinguishes "the call was wrong" from "the call was correct given what I knew, and here's the new information that would update it."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what would you have researched more?
slides.markdown:
A second common follow-up: "if you'd had unlimited time before this interview, what's the one thing you'd have researched more?" Answer with a genuine unknown specific to this problem — a real access pattern, an actual traffic distribution — rather than a generic "I'd study more system design."

A generic answer signals the self-critique was a rehearsed line, not real reflection on this design. A specific one — "I'd want the actual read/write ratio on the leaderboard before committing to eventual consistency" — shows the self-critique is genuinely about the problem you were just given.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: performing humility instead of critiquing
slides.markdown:
**Wrong move:** saying "I wouldn't change anything," or picking a trivial, low-stakes nitpick — a variable name, a minor endpoint shape — to perform humility without any real self-critique.

**Why it's wrong:** every real design involves trade-offs made under incomplete information, so claiming zero regrets either isn't true or means you haven't reflected on your own work. A trivial nitpick is worse in a different way: it looks like self-critique on the surface but reveals nothing about your judgment, which is exactly what the question is testing.

**Correct model:** name one decision made under genuine uncertainty, and say specifically what would change your mind.

Pick a decision you made under real uncertainty — not a trivial detail — and say what you'd revisit and what evidence would change your call. Ground it in a concrete example ("I chose eventual consistency for X because Y; I'd check Z before committing further"), not an abstract principle.

Then be ready for the two common follow-ups: defend why the original call was still right given what you knew then, and name one genuine unknown you'd have researched with more time. Both reward the same thing — specificity over a rehearsed, generic line.
